case_info.scenario: A 62-year-old Japanese man was diagnosed with submandibular salivary duct carcinoma (T4bN3cM0 according to Union for International Cancer Control, 8th edition). He had alcohol use disorder with facial flushing after small amounts of alcohol, suggestive of aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) deficiency—a common genetic polymorphism in East Asian populations. He underwent right neck dissection with skin resection, reconstruction using a pectoralis major flap, and adjuvant radiotherapy (66 Gy). He remained free of recurrence on regular clinical and computed tomography (CT) surveillance but continued daily heavy alcohol consumption. Three years later, he developed progressive frailty with 3 months of reduced oral intake. Neurologic examination revealed diminished superficial sensation, dysesthesia, and impaired proprioception in the lower extremities, consistent with sensory ataxia in a polyneuropathy pattern. Laboratory testing at that time showed macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 9.1 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]; mean corpuscular volume, 101.4 μm3(to convert to femtoliters, multiply by 1), and vitamin B12supplementation was initiated. In this clinical context, his sensory-dominant polyneuropathy was suspected to be related to chronic alcohol use and vitamin B12/folate deficiency. Spinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), performed to evaluate for structural causes of neurologic symptoms, revealed multiple hypointense lesions on T1-weighted images in the thoracolumbar spine (Figure 1A); similar findings were observed on T2-weighted imaging (image not shown). The corresponding CT image demonstrated mild hyperdensity with ill-defined margins without cortical destruction (Figure 1B). Given his oncologic history and the imaging findings, a CT-guided biopsy of the signal alteration in the T12 vertebral body was performed by an orthopedic spine surgeon for definitive diagnosis.

case_info.caption: A, Sagittal T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging shows multiple hypointense lesions in the thoracic and lumbar vertebrae. B, Sagittal computed tomography image (soft tissue window) demonstrates mild hyperdensity with ill-defined margins without cortical destruction.
case_info.explanation: Histological examination revealed trabecular bone without epithelial elements, and immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin (AE1/AE3) was negative. The bone marrow demonstrated normal trilineage hematopoiesis, with no evidence of malignancy. Although positron emission tomography (PET)/CT was not performed at that time, a retrospective review of a PET/CT scan obtained 3 years earlier revealed mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the thoracolumbar vertebral bodies (Figure 2). In the context of the patient’s clinical and imaging findings, these results are supportive of bone pseudometastasis.1This phenomenon has been predominantly reported in East Asian patients with esophageal cancer and, less frequently, in head and neck cancers.2,3 While biopsy remains the criterion standard for establishing the diagnosis, several imaging features can suggest bone pseudometastasis. Typical imaging shows hypointense lesions on T1/T2 MRI and mild hyperdensity without cortical destruction on CT.1Although these findings are nonspecific, the absence of aggressive features such as cortical destruction or soft tissue extension may help raise suspicion for a benign process. Serial imaging is also informative, as pseudometastatic lesions typically remain stable over time. In general, PET-CT may show mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake with lower standardized uptake values but cannot reliably distinguish pseudometastasis from true metastasis.1,3 The pathophysiology of bone pseudometastasis remains incompletely understood. Proposed mechanisms include alterations of the marrow microenvironment associated with chronic alcohol consumption and ALDH2 deficiency, which may influence hematopoietic activity, a hypothesis supported by frequent reports in Japanese patients with esophageal cancer, where ALDH2 deficiency is a known risk factor. Reported cases frequently demonstrated anemia or subsequent hematologic disorders such as myelodysplastic syndrome, suggesting that impaired or heterogeneous hematopoiesis and red marrow reconversion play central roles in its development.3Other plausible causes—malnutrition, prior irradiation, or intraosseous venous malformations—were unlikely: no irradiation history, no imaging evidence, and stability despite nutritional correction. Prior reports also showed benign hematopoietic marrow without tumor infiltration, consistent with the present case.1,2 Answer A was incorrect. In salivary duct carcinoma, approximately 15% develop bone metastases that can be lytic/sclerotic/mixed and mimic benignity; tissue diagnosis is essential.4Answer B was also incorrect.  Prostate metastases are typically osteoblastic with T1 low and T2 iso-low signal plus restricted diffusion, usually in older men with high prostate-specific antigen, which was absent here.5Answer C was incorrect as well. Myelofibrosis causes diffuse, symmetric low T1/T2 spinal signal, unlike this focal pattern.6 Recognizing these imaging patterns in context can avert unnecessary interventions and misdiagnosis; integrate clinicoradiologic correlation; and, when needed, pathologic confirmation or interval imaging to avoid missing true bone metastases.

next reply.

per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring

* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.

case_info.explanation: Histological examination revealed trabecular bone without epithelial elements, and immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin (AE1/AE3) was negative. The bone marrow demonstrated normal trilineage hematopoiesis, with no evidence of malignancy. Although positron emission tomography (PET)/CT was not performed at that time, a retrospective review of a PET/CT scan obtained 3 years earlier revealed mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the thoracolumbar vertebral bodies (Figure 2). In the context of the patient’s clinical and imaging findings, these results are supportive of bone pseudometastasis.1This phenomenon has been predominantly reported in East Asian patients with esophageal cancer and, less frequently, in head and neck cancers.2,3 While biopsy remains the criterion standard for establishing the diagnosis, several imaging features can suggest bone pseudometastasis. Typical imaging shows hypointense lesions on T1/T2 MRI and mild hyperdensity without cortical destruction on CT.1Although these findings are nonspecific, the absence of aggressive features such as cortical destruction or soft tissue extension may help raise suspicion for a benign process. Serial imaging is also informative, as pseudometastatic lesions typically remain stable over time. In general, PET-CT may show mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake with lower standardized uptake values but cannot reliably distinguish pseudometastasis from true metastasis.1,3 The pathophysiology of bone pseudometastasis remains incompletely understood. Proposed mechanisms include alterations of the marrow microenvironment associated with chronic alcohol consumption and ALDH2 deficiency, which may influence hematopoietic activity, a hypothesis supported by frequent reports in Japanese patients with esophageal cancer, where ALDH2 deficiency is a known risk factor. Reported cases frequently demonstrated anemia or subsequent hematologic disorders such as myelodysplastic syndrome, suggesting that impaired or heterogeneous hematopoiesis and red marrow reconversion play central roles in its development.3Other plausible causes—malnutrition, prior irradiation, or intraosseous venous malformations—were unlikely: no irradiation history, no imaging evidence, and stability despite nutritional correction. Prior reports also showed benign hematopoietic marrow without tumor infiltration, consistent with the present case.1,2 Answer A was incorrect. In salivary duct carcinoma, approximately 15% develop bone metastases that can be lytic/sclerotic/mixed and mimic benignity; tissue diagnosis is essential.4Answer B was also incorrect.  Prostate metastases are typically osteoblastic with T1 low and T2 iso-low signal plus restricted diffusion, usually in older men with high prostate-specific antigen, which was absent here.5Answer C was incorrect as well. Myelofibrosis causes diffuse, symmetric low T1/T2 spinal signal, unlike this focal pattern.6 Recognizing these imaging patterns in context can avert unnecessary interventions and misdiagnosis; integrate clinicoradiologic correlation; and, when needed, pathologic confirmation or interval imaging to avoid missing true bone metastases.

[Clinical case]
A 62-year-old Japanese man was diagnosed with submandibular salivary duct carcinoma (T4bN3cM0 according to Union for International Cancer Control, 8th edition). He had alcohol use disorder with facial flushing after small amounts of alcohol, suggestive of aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) deficiency—a common genetic polymorphism in East Asian populations. He underwent right neck dissection with skin resection, reconstruction using a pectoralis major flap, and adjuvant radiotherapy (66 Gy). He remained free of recurrence on regular clinical and computed tomography (CT) surveillance but continued daily heavy alcohol consumption. Three years later, he developed progressive frailty with 3 months of reduced oral intake. Neurologic examination revealed diminished superficial sensation, dysesthesia, and impaired proprioception in the lower extremities, consistent with sensory ataxia in a polyneuropathy pattern. Laboratory testing at that time showed macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 9.1 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]; mean corpuscular volume, 101.4 μm3(to convert to femtoliters, multiply by 1), and vitamin B12supplementation was initiated. In this clinical context, his sensory-dominant polyneuropathy was suspected to be related to chronic alcohol use and vitamin B12/folate deficiency. Spinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), performed to evaluate for structural causes of neurologic symptoms, revealed multiple hypointense lesions on T1-weighted images in the thoracolumbar spine (Figure 1A); similar findings were observed on T2-weighted imaging (image not shown). The corresponding CT image demonstrated mild hyperdensity with ill-defined margins without cortical destruction (Figure 1B). Given his oncologic history and the imaging findings, a CT-guided biopsy of the signal alteration in the T12 vertebral body was performed by an orthopedic spine surgeon for definitive diagnosis.

case_info.explanation: Histological examination revealed trabecular bone without epithelial elements, and immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin (AE1/AE3) was negative. The bone marrow demonstrated normal trilineage hematopoiesis, with no evidence of malignancy. Although positron emission tomography (PET)/CT was not performed at that time, a retrospective review of a PET/CT scan obtained 3 years earlier revealed mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the thoracolumbar vertebral bodies (Figure 2). In the context of the patient’s clinical and imaging findings, these results are supportive of bone pseudometastasis.1This phenomenon has been predominantly reported in East Asian patients with esophageal cancer and, less frequently, in head and neck cancers.2,3 While biopsy remains the criterion standard for establishing the diagnosis, several imaging features can suggest bone pseudometastasis. Typical imaging shows hypointense lesions on T1/T2 MRI and mild hyperdensity without cortical destruction on CT.1Although these findings are nonspecific, the absence of aggressive features such as cortical destruction or soft tissue extension may help raise suspicion for a benign process. Serial imaging is also informative, as pseudometastatic lesions typically remain stable over time. In general, PET-CT may show mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake with lower standardized uptake values but cannot reliably distinguish pseudometastasis from true metastasis.1,3 The pathophysiology of bone pseudometastasis remains incompletely understood. Proposed mechanisms include alterations of the marrow microenvironment associated with chronic alcohol consumption and ALDH2 deficiency, which may influence hematopoietic activity, a hypothesis supported by frequent reports in Japanese patients with esophageal cancer, where ALDH2 deficiency is a known risk factor. Reported cases frequently demonstrated anemia or subsequent hematologic disorders such as myelodysplastic syndrome, suggesting that impaired or heterogeneous hematopoiesis and red marrow reconversion play central roles in its development.3Other plausible causes—malnutrition, prior irradiation, or intraosseous venous malformations—were unlikely: no irradiation history, no imaging evidence, and stability despite nutritional correction. Prior reports also showed benign hematopoietic marrow without tumor infiltration, consistent with the present case.1,2 Answer A was incorrect. In salivary duct carcinoma, approximately 15% develop bone metastases that can be lytic/sclerotic/mixed and mimic benignity; tissue diagnosis is essential.4Answer B was also incorrect.  Prostate metastases are typically osteoblastic with T1 low and T2 iso-low signal plus restricted diffusion, usually in older men with high prostate-specific antigen, which was absent here.5Answer C was incorrect as well. Myelofibrosis causes diffuse, symmetric low T1/T2 spinal signal, unlike this focal pattern.6 Recognizing these imaging patterns in context can avert unnecessary interventions and misdiagnosis; integrate clinicoradiologic correlation; and, when needed, pathologic confirmation or interval imaging to avoid missing true bone metastases.

You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.

4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 62-year-old Japanese man was diagnosed with submandibular salivary duct carcinoma (T4bN3cM0 according to Union for International Cancer Control, 8th edition). He had alcohol use disorder with facial flushing after small amounts of alcohol, suggestive of aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) deficiency—a common genetic polymorphism in East Asian populations. He underwent right neck dissection with skin resection, reconstruction using a pectoralis major flap, and adjuvant radiotherapy (66 Gy). He remained free of recurrence on regular clinical and computed tomography (CT) surveillance but continued daily heavy alcohol consumption. Three years later, he developed progressive frailty with 3 months of reduced oral intake. Neurologic examination revealed diminished superficial sensation, dysesthesia, and impaired proprioception in the lower extremities, consistent with sensory ataxia in a polyneuropathy pattern. Laboratory testing at that time showed macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 9.1 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]; mean corpuscular volume, 101.4 μm3(to convert to femtoliters, multiply by 1), and vitamin B12supplementation was initiated. In this clinical context, his sensory-dominant polyneuropathy was suspected to be related to chronic alcohol use and vitamin B12/folate deficiency. Spinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), performed to evaluate for structural causes of neurologic symptoms, revealed multiple hypointense lesions on T1-weighted images in the thoracolumbar spine (Figure 1A); similar findings were observed on T2-weighted imaging (image not shown). The corresponding CT image demonstrated mild hyperdensity with ill-defined margins without cortical destruction (Figure 1B). Given his oncologic history and the imaging findings, a CT-guided biopsy of the signal alteration in the T12 vertebral body was performed by an orthopedic spine surgeon for definitive diagnosis.

1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

The corresponding CT image demonstrated mild hyperdensity with ill-defined margins without cortical destruction (Figure 1B). Given his oncologic history and the imaging findings, a CT-guided biopsy of the signal alteration in the T12 vertebral body was performed by an orthopedic spine surgeon for definitive diagnosis.

case_info.explanation: Histological examination revealed trabecular bone without epithelial elements, and immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin (AE1/AE3) was negative. The bone marrow demonstrated normal trilineage hematopoiesis, with no evidence of malignancy. Although positron emission tomography (PET)/CT was not performed at that time, a retrospective review of a PET/CT scan obtained 3 years earlier revealed mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the thoracolumbar vertebral bodies (Figure 2). In the context of the patient’s clinical and imaging findings, these results are supportive of bone pseudometastasis.1This phenomenon has been predominantly reported in East Asian patients with esophageal cancer and, less frequently, in head and neck cancers.2,3 While biopsy remains the criterion standard for establishing the diagnosis, several imaging features can suggest bone pseudometastasis. Typical imaging shows hypointense lesions on T1/T2 MRI and mild hyperdensity without cortical destruction on CT.1Although these findings are nonspecific, the absence of aggressive features such as cortical destruction or soft tissue extension may help raise suspicion for a benign process. Serial imaging is also informative, as pseudometastatic lesions typically remain stable over time. In general, PET-CT may show mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake with lower standardized uptake values but cannot reliably distinguish pseudometastasis from true metastasis.1,3 The pathophysiology of bone pseudometastasis remains incompletely understood. Proposed mechanisms include alterations of the marrow microenvironment associated with chronic alcohol consumption and ALDH2 deficiency, which may influence hematopoietic activity, a hypothesis supported by frequent reports in Japanese patients with esophageal cancer, where ALDH2 deficiency is a known risk factor. Reported cases frequently demonstrated anemia or subsequent hematologic disorders such as myelodysplastic syndrome, suggesting that impaired or heterogeneous hematopoiesis and red marrow reconversion play central roles in its development.3Other plausible causes—malnutrition, prior irradiation, or intraosseous venous malformations—were unlikely: no irradiation history, no imaging evidence, and stability despite nutritional correction. Prior reports also showed benign hematopoietic marrow without tumor infiltration, consistent with the present case.1,2 Answer A was incorrect. In salivary duct carcinoma, approximately 15% develop bone metastases that can be lytic/sclerotic/mixed and mimic benignity; tissue diagnosis is essential.4Answer B was also incorrect.  Prostate metastases are typically osteoblastic with T1 low and T2 iso-low signal plus restricted diffusion, usually in older men with high prostate-specific antigen, which was absent here.5Answer C was incorrect as well. Myelofibrosis causes diffuse, symmetric low T1/T2 spinal signal, unlike this focal pattern.6 Recognizing these imaging patterns in context can avert unnecessary interventions and misdiagnosis; integrate clinicoradiologic correlation; and, when needed, pathologic confirmation or interval imaging to avoid missing true bone metastases.

case_info.explanation: Histological examination revealed trabecular bone without epithelial elements, and immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin (AE1/AE3) was negative. The bone marrow demonstrated normal trilineage hematopoiesis, with no evidence of malignancy. Although positron emission tomography (PET)/CT was not performed at that time, a retrospective review of a PET/CT scan obtained 3 years earlier revealed mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the thoracolumbar vertebral bodies (Figure 2). In the context of the patient’s clinical and imaging findings, these results are supportive of bone pseudometastasis.1This phenomenon has been predominantly reported in East Asian patients with esophageal cancer and, less frequently, in head and neck cancers.2,3 While biopsy remains the criterion standard for establishing the diagnosis, several imaging features can suggest bone pseudometastasis. Typical imaging shows hypointense lesions on T1/T2 MRI and mild hyperdensity without cortical destruction on CT.1Although these findings are nonspecific, the absence of aggressive features such as cortical destruction or soft tissue extension may help raise suspicion for a benign process. Serial imaging is also informative, as pseudometastatic lesions typically remain stable over time. In general, PET-CT may show mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake with lower standardized uptake values but cannot reliably distinguish pseudometastasis from true metastasis.1,3 The pathophysiology of bone pseudometastasis remains incompletely understood. Proposed mechanisms include alterations of the marrow microenvironment associated with chronic alcohol consumption and ALDH2 deficiency, which may influence hematopoietic activity, a hypothesis supported by frequent reports in Japanese patients with esophageal cancer, where ALDH2 deficiency is a known risk factor. Reported cases frequently demonstrated anemia or subsequent hematologic disorders such as myelodysplastic syndrome, suggesting that impaired or heterogeneous hematopoiesis and red marrow reconversion play central roles in its development.3Other plausible causes—malnutrition, prior irradiation, or intraosseous venous malformations—were unlikely: no irradiation history, no imaging evidence, and stability despite nutritional correction. In salivary duct carcinoma, approximately 15% develop bone metastases that can be lytic/sclerotic/mixed and mimic benignity; tissue diagnosis is essential.4Answer B was also incorrect.  Prostate metastases are typically osteoblastic with T1 low and T2 iso-low signal plus restricted diffusion, usually in older men with high prostate-specific antigen, which was absent here.5Answer C was incorrect as well. A 62-year-old Japanese man was diagnosed with submandibular salivary duct carcinoma (T4bN3cM0 according to Union for International Cancer Control, 8th edition). He had alcohol use disorder with facial flushing after small amounts of alcohol, suggestive of aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) deficiency—a common genetic polymorphism in East Asian populations. He remained free of recurrence on regular clinical and computed tomography (CT) surveillance but continued daily heavy alcohol consumption. Three years later, he developed progressive frailty with 3 months of reduced oral intake. Neurologic examination revealed diminished superficial sensation, dysesthesia, and impaired proprioception in the lower extremities, consistent with sensory ataxia in a polyneuropathy pattern. Laboratory testing at that time showed macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 9.1 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]; mean corpuscular volume, 101.4 μm3(to convert to femtoliters, multiply by 1), and vitamin B12supplementation was initiated. In this clinical context, his sensory-dominant polyneuropathy was suspected to be related to chronic alcohol use and vitamin B12/folate deficiency. Spinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), performed to evaluate for structural causes of neurologic symptoms, revealed multiple hypointense lesions on T1-weighted images in the thoracolumbar spine (Figure 1A); similar findings were observed on T2-weighted imaging (image not shown). The corresponding CT image demonstrated mild hyperdensity with ill-defined margins without cortical destruction (Figure 1B). Given his oncologic history and the imaging findings, a CT-guided biopsy of the signal alteration in the T12 vertebral body was performed by an orthopedic spine surgeon for definitive diagnosis.

case_info.explanation: Histological examination revealed trabecular bone without epithelial elements, and immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin (AE1/AE3) was negative. The bone marrow demonstrated normal trilineage hematopoiesis, with no evidence of malignancy. Although positron emission tomography (PET)/CT was not performed at that time, a retrospective review of a PET/CT scan obtained 3 years earlier revealed mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the thoracolumbar vertebral bodies (Figure 2). In the context of the patient’s clinical and imaging findings, these results are supportive of bone pseudometastasis.1This phenomenon has been predominantly reported in East Asian patients with esophageal cancer and, less frequently, in head and neck cancers.2,3 While biopsy remains the criterion standard for establishing the diagnosis, several imaging features can suggest bone pseudometastasis. Typical imaging shows hypointense lesions on T1/T2 MRI and mild hyperdensity without cortical destruction on CT.1Although these findings are nonspecific, the absence of aggressive features such as cortical destruction or soft tissue extension may help raise suspicion for a benign process. Serial imaging is also informative, as pseudometastatic lesions typically remain stable over time. In general, PET-CT may show mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake with lower standardized uptake values but cannot reliably distinguish pseudometastasis from true metastasis.1,3 The pathophysiology of bone pseudometastasis remains incompletely understood. Proposed mechanisms include alterations of the marrow microenvironment associated with chronic alcohol consumption and ALDH2 deficiency, which may influence hematopoietic activity, a hypothesis supported by frequent reports in Japanese patients with esophageal cancer, where ALDH2 deficiency is a known risk factor. Reported cases frequently demonstrated anemia or subsequent hematologic disorders such as myelodysplastic syndrome, suggesting that impaired or heterogeneous hematopoiesis and red marrow reconversion play central roles in its development.3Other plausible causes—malnutrition, prior irradiation, or intraosseous venous malformations—were unlikely: no irradiation history, no imaging evidence, and stability despite nutritional correction. Prior reports also showed benign hematopoietic marrow without tumor infiltration, consistent with the present case.1,2 Answer A was incorrect. In salivary duct carcinoma, approximately 15% develop bone metastases that can be lytic/sclerotic/mixed and mimic benignity; tissue diagnosis is essential.4Answer B was also incorrect.  Prostate metastases are typically osteoblastic with T1 low and T2 iso-low signal plus restricted diffusion, usually in older men with high prostate-specific antigen, which was absent here.5Answer C was incorrect as well. Myelofibrosis causes diffuse, symmetric low T1/T2 spinal signal, unlike this focal pattern.6 Recognizing these imaging patterns in context can avert unnecessary interventions and misdiagnosis; integrate clinicoradiologic correlation; and, when needed, pathologic confirmation or interval imaging to avoid missing true bone metastases.

He had alcohol use disorder with facial flushing after small amounts of alcohol, suggestive of aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) deficiency—a common genetic polymorphism in East Asian populations. He underwent right neck dissection with skin resection, reconstruction using a pectoralis major flap, and adjuvant radiotherapy (66 Gy). He remained free of recurrence on regular clinical and computed tomography (CT) surveillance but continued daily heavy alcohol consumption. Three years later, he developed progressive frailty with 3 months of reduced oral intake. Neurologic examination revealed diminished superficial sensation, dysesthesia, and impaired proprioception in the lower extremities, consistent with sensory ataxia in a polyneuropathy pattern. Laboratory testing at that time showed macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 9.1 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]; mean corpuscular volume, 101.4 μm3(to convert to femtoliters, multiply by 1), and vitamin B12supplementation was initiated. In this clinical context, his sensory-dominant polyneuropathy was suspected to be related to chronic alcohol use and vitamin B12/folate deficiency. Spinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), performed to evaluate for structural causes of neurologic symptoms, revealed multiple hypointense lesions on T1-weighted images in the thoracolumbar spine (Figure 1A); similar findings were observed on T2-weighted imaging (image not shown). The corresponding CT image demonstrated mild hyperdensity with ill-defined margins without cortical destruction (Figure 1B). Given his oncologic history and the imaging findings, a CT-guided biopsy of the signal alteration in the T12 vertebral body was performed by an orthopedic spine surgeon for definitive diagnosis.
